title: FDA Investigates New Cyclospora Outbreak as Parasite Cases Top 4,000 Nationwide
excerpt: A fourth outbreak cluster involving 72 people has been identified, with the contaminated product still unknown. The crisis deepens even as Taylor Farms' lettuce test result was declared a false positive.
body:
• The FDA announced a fourth active cyclospora outbreak cluster on July 22, involving at least 72 people, with the source product not yet identified.
  • Nationwide, the CDC has confirmed 4,173 cyclosporiasis cases across 41 states since May 1, with over 7,400 additional suspected infections under review and at least 308 hospitalizations.
  • The largest cluster — more than 1,600 cases — has been linked to shredded iceberg lettuce from Taylor Farms served at Taco Bell locations in five Midwestern states, though a lab test on the lettuce was later declared a false positive.
  • Mexico's health ministry says its own tests on Taylor Farms lettuce and water samples found no traces of the Cyclospora parasite.

A Fourth Outbreak Cluster Emerges

The Food and Drug Administration disclosed Wednesday that it is investigating a newly identified cyclospora outbreak that has sickened at least 72 people across the United States. The agency said it has launched traceback efforts to determine which food product is responsible, but has not yet pinpointed the source.

https://x.com/winknews/status/2080447128434806936

"A new outbreak of Cyclospora linked to a not yet identified product has been added to the table. FDA has initiated traceback," the agency said in an updated advisory.

The cluster is one of at least four active cyclosporiasis investigations the FDA is currently running — a sign that the parasitic illness, which surges during spring and summer months, is proving unusually difficult to contain this year.

A Growing National Health Crisis

The numbers paint a stark picture. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has confirmed 4,173 domestically acquired cyclosporiasis cases across 41 states since May 1. Beyond confirmed cases, more than 7,400 additional reported infections are still awaiting laboratory confirmation. At least 308 people have been hospitalized.

The largest of the four active clusters has been traced to shredded iceberg lettuce supplied by Taylor Farms, a California-based produce company, and served at Taco Bell restaurants in Indiana, Kentucky, Michigan, Ohio, and West Virginia. That cluster alone accounts for more than 1,600 cases.

Taylor Fresh Foods announced a voluntary recall of iceberg lettuce sourced from its processing facilities in central Mexico, covering products distributed across 27 states. Taco Bell said it has removed the potentially impacted lettuce from affected locations and replaced the ingredient.

False Positive Complicates the Investigation

The Taylor Farms investigation took a confusing turn last week. The FDA initially reported a positive cyclospora test result on a sample of the company's shredded iceberg lettuce. Within a day, the agency reversed course and declared it a false positive.

"False positives are not common. In fact, it's very difficult to detect this parasite in food. Unlike bacteria, this parasite cannot be cultured using conventional laboratory techniques."

— Donald Prater, FDA Acting Deputy Commissioner for Food

The FDA said its import screening program uses highly sensitive polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing methods, but the complexity of detecting Cyclospora in food led to the erroneous result. As of July 19, the agency confirmed there are no verified positive product samples for the parasite.

Mexico's health ministry added another layer to the dispute on Thursday, announcing that its own real-time PCR analysis of 10 samples from Taylor Farms' raw materials and finished products found no traces of Cyclospora cayetanensis.

Despite the revised test result, the FDA maintained that epidemiological evidence linking the outbreak to Taylor Farms remains "overwhelming." The agency said its traceback investigation and outbreak data "continue to converge on shredded iceberg lettuce from Taylor Farms locations in central Mexico."

What Indian Americans Should Know

Cyclospora cayetanensis is a microscopic parasite that contaminates food — most commonly fresh produce — when it comes into contact with water tainted by human feces. The illness it causes, cyclosporiasis, triggers watery diarrhea, severe stomach cramps, bloating, and vomiting that can persist for weeks if untreated. Symptoms typically appear about a week after exposure but can take up to two weeks to manifest.

For Indian American families who regularly consume fresh salads and eat at fast-food chains, the outbreak is a reminder to stay vigilant about produce sourcing. Health officials advise thorough handwashing with soap and water before handling food — alcohol-based hand sanitizers do not kill the cyclospora parasite. The FDA recommends that consumers monitor its outbreak advisory page for updates on which products may be affected.

What Comes Next

With four active outbreak clusters and thousands of cases still under review, investigators face a sprawling challenge. Michigan, the hardest-hit state, has not yet identified a definitive source for its infections. Authorities there have pointed to lettuce and salad greens as a risk factor but say there is not enough evidence to assign blame or rule out multiple simultaneous outbreaks.

The FDA said it will continue collecting and analyzing product samples while working with Taylor Farms and state officials to ensure implicated products have been pulled from the market. For the newest 72-person cluster, the traceback investigation is just beginning — and consumers may not get answers for weeks.
